questions.question: How does FastAPI convert an int path parameter?
expected_facts: An int annotation makes the path value arrive as an integer after conversion.

evidence.text: Notice that the value your function received (and returned) is 3, as a Python int, not a string "3".
So, with that type declaration, FastAPI gives you automatic request "parsing".

questions.question: Why should a fixed path operation appear before a parameterized route?
expected_facts: Path operations are evaluated in order, so a fixed route must precede a matching parameter route.

evidence.text: And then you can also have a path /users/{user_id} to get data about a specific user by some user ID.
Because path operations are evaluated in order, you need to make sure that the path for /users/me is declared before the one for /users/{user_id}:

questions.question: How do I give skip and limit query parameters default values?
expected_facts: Defaults in function parameters supply values when query parameters are omitted.

evidence.text: As query parameters are not a fixed part of a path, they can be optional and can have default values.
In the example above they have default values of skip=0 and limit=10.
skip=20: because you set it in the URL
limit=10: because that was the default value

questions.question: Can a boolean query parameter accept values such as yes or on?
expected_facts: The documented boolean conversion accepts several true-like query strings.

evidence.text: You can also declare bool types, and they will be converted:
http://127.0.0.1:8000/items/foo?short=on

questions.question: How do I define a JSON request body with Pydantic?
expected_facts: Declare a BaseModel subclass with annotated fields and use it as a route parameter.

evidence.text: Then you declare your data model as a class that inherits from BaseModel.

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel


class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    description: str | None = None
    price: float
    tax: float | None = None


app = FastAPI()


@app.post("/items/")
async def create_item(item: Item):
    return item

questions.question: Can one endpoint use a request body with path and query parameters?
expected_facts: The documented endpoint combines path parameters, an Item body model, and optional query data.

evidence.text: You can also declare body, path and query parameters, all at the same time.

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel


class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    description: str | None = None
    price: float
    tax: float | None = None


app = FastAPI()


@app.put("/items/{item_id}")
async def update_item(item_id: int, item: Item, q: str | None = None):
    result = {"item_id": item_id, **item.model_dump()}
    if q:
        result.update({"q": q})
    return result

questions.question: What does response_model do to returned data?
expected_facts: The declared response model validates, converts, documents, and filters the returned output.

evidence.text: FastAPI will use this response_model to do all the data documentation, validation, etc. and also to convert and filter the output data to its type declaration.

questions.question: How can I avoid returning an input password in my response?
expected_facts: Use a distinct output model that omits the password field.

evidence.text: We can instead create an input model with the plaintext password and an output model without it:

from typing import Any

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr

app = FastAPI()


class UserIn(BaseModel):
    username: str
    password: str
    email: EmailStr
    full_name: str | None = None


class UserOut(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: EmailStr
    full_name: str | None = None


@app.post("/user/", response_model=UserOut)
async def create_user(user: UserIn) -> Any:
    return user

questions.question: Which takes priority when both a return annotation and response_model are declared?
expected_facts: The response_model takes priority over the return type annotation.

evidence.text: If you declare both a return type and a response_model, the response_model will take priority and be used by FastAPI.

questions.question: How do I receive a shared dependency value in a route?
expected_facts: Declare a parameter with Depends on the dependency function.

evidence.text: The same way you use Body, Query, etc. with your path operation function parameters, use Depends with a new parameter:

from typing import Annotated

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI

app = FastAPI()


async def common_parameters(q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
    return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}


@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]):
    return commons


@app.get("/users/")
async def read_users(commons: Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]):
    return commons

questions.question: How do I reuse an Annotated dependency declaration across routes?
expected_facts: Assign an Annotated dependency type to an alias and reuse it in route signatures.

evidence.text: But because we are using Annotated, we can store that Annotated value in a variable and use it in multiple places:

from typing import Annotated

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI

app = FastAPI()


async def common_parameters(q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
    return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}


CommonsDep = Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]


@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: CommonsDep):
    return commons


@app.get("/users/")
async def read_users(commons: CommonsDep):
    return commons

questions.question: How do I close a database resource in a dependency with yield?
expected_facts: Yield the resource inside try and close it in finally after its use.

evidence.text: For example, you could use this to create a database session and close it after finishing.

async def get_db():
    db = DBSession()
    try:
        yield db
    finally:
        db.close()

questions.question: How can a dependency with yield translate a caught exception into HTTPException?
expected_facts: Catch the exception in an except block and raise HTTPException, as in the documented dependency.

evidence.text: You can also use except to catch the exception that was raised and do something with it.
For example, you can raise a different exception, like HTTPException.

questions.question: How do I call FastAPI endpoints from a test without starting a live server?
expected_facts: Use TestClient with the application and regular test functions.

evidence.text: Create a TestClient by passing your FastAPI application to it.
Create functions with a name that starts with test_ (this is a standard pytest convention).
Notice that the testing functions are normal def, not async def.

questions.question: How do I check a response status code and JSON body in a test?
expected_facts: Call the endpoint through TestClient and assert its status_code and json result.
